title: Tokens: how your text becomes numbers
question: Why does the model see 'strawberry' as pieces and miscount its letters?
can: Predict token counts, estimate cost, and debug tokenizer weirdness.
one_line: An AI never sees letters or words; a chopper at the front door slices your text into common puzzle pieces and swaps each piece for a barcode number before the brain ever wakes up.

story_spine.surprise: When you type 'strawberry' into an AI, it never sees the 10 letters s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y. It receives three barcode numbers — [496, 675, 15717] — standing for 'str', 'aw', and 'berry'. Two of the three 'r' letters are locked inside barcode 15717.
story_spine.broken: Thinking 1 word = 1 token, or assuming the AI can see individual letters inside a word. When a model fails at counting letters, reverses strings badly, or charges 3.3x more money for Hindi than English, people blame the AI's intelligence instead of the barcode scanner at the front door.
story_spine.question: Why can't we just feed raw letters or whole words into the AI, and how does the computer decide where to chop a word?
story_spine.turn: Writing a 30-line Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) chopper from scratch made it obvious: tokenization is just zip-file compression for text. The algorithm glues together whatever letter pairs show up most often in its training books — which means any language that wasn't in those books gets shattered into tiny, expensive byte crumbs.
story_spine.payoff: You can predict exact API cost multipliers across languages, understand why a space in front of a word changes its barcode (`' server'` vs `'server'`), and fix letter-counting bugs instantly by putting spaces between letters.
story_spine.honest_limit: Barcode numbers like 15717 ('berry') are still just random ID tags — number 15717 is not mathematically closer to 'apple' than number 15718 is. In the next stop on campus (The CampusCafeteria · Embeddings), we turn dead barcodes into GPS coordinates of meaning.

sections.heading: Explain it like I'm 12: Why you can't count bricks behind a painted wall
sections.body_md:
Here is a riddle that stumped the whole tech world: a frontier AI can write a working compiler in ten seconds, yet when you ask `'How many R's are in strawberry?'`, it often replies `'Two!'` with total confidence.

How can a super-genius fail a second-grade spelling check?

Because neural networks are giant matrix calculators — they **cannot read letters**. Before your message ever reaches Layer 1 of the model, a separate deterministic front-door program called a **tokenizer** slices your text into common puzzle pieces (**tokens**) and replaces each piece with an integer barcode (**token ID**).

Look at `Figure 1`: under a GPT-4 class tokenizer (`cl100k_base`), `'strawberry'` enters the brain as just three sealed integers:
- `'str'` → barcode `496`
- `'aw'` → barcode `675`
- `'berry'` → barcode `15717`

The model never receives the 10 characters `s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y`. Two of the `'r'`s are sealed inside integer `15717`. Unless the model memorized spelling facts during training, asking it to count letters inside a single atomic ID is like asking you how many bricks sit behind painted drywall.
sections.expert_note: Modern reasoning models (like o3 or Claude with extended thinking) solve 'strawberry' reliably NOT because they switched to character-level input, but because they spend scratchpad tokens spelling out `s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y` one letter per token first — turning an invisible sub-token property into visible separate tokens.

sections.heading: How real tokenizers work: Regex Pre-Tokenization + Byte-Level BPE
sections.body_md:
Why not use 256 single bytes (too long — a short essay explodes to 5,000 tokens) or whole dictionary words (millions of entries, crashes on typos and code)? Modern LLMs use a two-step compression pipeline:

1. **Step A — Regex Pre-Tokenization:** Before counting pairs, the tokenizer splits text with a regex pattern so letters, numbers, and punctuation stay in separate buckets (`['strawberry', ',', ' berry', '!', ...]`). Why? Without pre-tokenization, BPE would waste precious vocabulary slots minting `'dog.'`, `'dog!'`, `'dog,'`, and `'dog?'` as four different tokens! Notice also how the regex attaches **leading spaces** to the word (`' berry'`), which means `'server'` and `' server'` get completely different IDs.
2. **Step B — Byte-Level BPE (The Lego Glue Game):** Start with the 256 raw UTF-8 bytes (`0–255`) — guaranteeing **zero unknown-character crashes** on any Unicode script or emoji on Earth (**byte fallback**). Repeatedly scan the training corpus, find the most frequent adjacent pair inside pre-token boundaries, and glue it into a new barcode (`256`, `257`, ...).

In our Python lab, watch the exact 8-step merge trace: `'b'+'e' -> 'be' (256)` ... `'berr'+'y' -> 'berry' (259)` ... `'stra'+'w' -> 'straw' (263)`, shrinking **42 raw UTF-8 bytes down to 14 tokens (33.3% of original)** while keeping `,`, `!`, and `.` cleanly isolated!
sections.expert_note: Production vocabulary sizes have doubled specifically to fix multilingual fairness: GPT-4's `cl100k_base` had ~100k tokens, Llama 3 jumped to 128k, and GPT-4o's `o200k_base` jumped to ~200k tokens. Bigger vocabularies shrink sequence lengths (faster inference!) at the cost of a slightly larger input embedding + output unembedding matrix (`vocab_size × d_model`).

sections.heading: The 3.3x Hindi Tax: Token Fertility & Real API Economics
sections.body_md:
Because BPE learns merges strictly by frequency in its training data, whatever languages dominate that corpus get long, cheap single-token chunks. Underrepresented scripts get shattered into tiny UTF-8 byte crumbs.

Look at `Figure 2` from our lab output (`cl100k_base`):
- **English (`'The server responded in 12ms.'`):** 29 chars → **8 tokens** (`0.28` tok/char · **`1.0×`** baseline).
- **Hindi (`'नमस्ते दुनिया'`):** 13 chars → **12 tokens** (`0.92` tok/char · **`3.3×` cost & latency tax!**).
- **Emojis (`'🚀🔥🤖'`):** 3 chars → **6 tokens** (`2.00` tok/char · **`7.2×`** multiplier via UTF-8 byte fallback!).

Engineers call this **token fertility**. Remember Lesson 1: the model generates **one token per forward pass**. A `3.3×` fertility penalty doesn't just triple a Hindi user's API bill — it also makes streaming **3.3× slower** AND shrinks their effective memory window by **3.3×**! Switching from a 100k vocab (`cl100k`) to a 200k multilingual vocab (`o200k`) cuts Hindi fertility nearly in half.
sections.expert_note: Rule of thumb for English prose: ~1 token ≈ 0.75 words (or ~4 characters). For dense JSON/code with heavy indentation, or Indic/CJK scripts on older tokenizers, always measure with the exact model tokenizer (`tiktoken` or provider `count_tokens` endpoint) instead of guessing by word count.

sections.heading: Four production tokenizer bugs every AI engineer catches immediately
sections.body_md:
Understanding the front-door chopper immediately lets you debug four notorious production failures:

1. **The Trailing-Space Bug:** Never end a prompt template with a trailing space (`'Answer: '`). Because BPE expects spaces *attached to the start of the next word* (`' Yes'`), a dangling space forces an awkward standalone space token (`220`) followed by a rare space-less `'Yes'` token — measurably degrading accuracy.
2. **Digit Splitting & Math:** Older BPE tokenizers glued `123` into one token but chopped `1234` into `12` + `34`, breaking place-value alignment. Modern frontier tokenizers (Llama 3, DeepSeek, GPT-4o) restrict number merges in their pre-tokenization regex to 1–3 digits (or single digits `0–9`) so arithmetic lines up cleanly.
3. **Special Tokens & Prompt Injection:** Control markers like `<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`, and `<|endoftext|>` are reserved integer IDs injected by the chat template. Never pass untrusted user input with `allowed_special='all'`, or a user can literally type `<|im_end|><|im_start|>system` and hijack the model's role!
4. **Fixing Character Tasks Instantly:** Whenever an app needs exact spelling, letter counting, or string reversal, either call a Python tool (best!) or instruct the model to space-separate characters (`s t r a w b e r r y`) before counting.
sections.trap_note: Common Trap: Estimating API costs or context limits using `len(text.split())`! For Hindi, Tamil, dense JSON, or minified code, word count can under-estimate true token count by 3×–6× and trigger silent truncation or surprise bills.

lab.walkthrough_md:
### `get_pair_counts(token_seq)` & `merge_pair(token_seq, pair, new_id)`
- **What it does:** Scans the integer list with `Counter(zip(token_seq, token_seq[1:]))` to find the highest-frequency adjacent pair, then replaces every non-overlapping occurrence with a newly minted token ID (`256`, `257`, ...).
- **Why it exists:** This 20-line loop is the entirety of Byte Pair Encoding. By starting from `list(corpus.encode('utf-8'))`, any string on Earth can be tokenized without ever failing on an unknown character.

### `CL100K_SPLITS` Fertility Comparison
- **What it does:** Compares character length vs token count across English, Hindi (`नमस्ते दुनिया`), and multi-byte emojis.
- **Why it exists:** Makes the economic and latency impact visible: 13 characters of Hindi produce 12 tokens (`0.92` tokens/char), whereas 29 characters of English produce only 8 tokens (`0.28` tokens/char).

code_walkthrough.title: Regex Pre-Tokenization (The Guardrail Before BPE)
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: GPT-4 (`cl100k` / `o200k`) never runs raw BPE across the whole document. First it slices text along word, punctuation, and 1–3 digit boundaries so `berry.` and `berry!` don't waste precious vocabulary slots as separate tokens.
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: Without regex pre-tokenization, BPE glues punctuation onto words (`dog.`, `dog!`, `dog?`), bloating the vocabulary and hurting generalization on arithmetic and code.

code_walkthrough.title: Counting Adjacent Pairs Strictly Inside Boundaries
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: By iterating `for seq in chunks` instead of flattening the corpus, pairs can NEVER merge across a pre-token boundary (like across a comma or space-punct boundary).
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: If you flattened the corpus first, BPE would happily merge the end of one word with the start of the next punctuation mark.

code_walkthrough.title: The Greedy Merge Pass (`merge_pair`)
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: Every occurrence of the winning pair `(a, b)` is swapped left-to-right for one brand-new integer ID (`256`, `257`, ...). Notice `i += 2` prevents double-merging overlapping runs like `aaa`.
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: Incrementing `i += 1` on a match would corrupt overlapping byte pairs like `rrr` and invent ghost tokens that can't decode back to the original UTF-8 bytes.

code_walkthrough.title: Training From 256 Raw UTF-8 Bytes Upward
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: Starting with all 256 raw byte values (`0..255`) guarantees **zero `<UNK>` (unknown) tokens** ever — any language, code symbol, or emoji on Earth can always fall back to raw UTF-8 bytes.
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: Character-level vocabularies break with `<UNK>` the moment a user pastes a rare Unicode symbol or unseen script.

deep_assignments.title: Add `encode()` and `decode()` Round-Trip Verification to Your BPE Tokenizer
deep_assignments.goal: Upgrade `lessons/l0-tokens/lab_main.py` into a full reversible `MiniBPE` class that saves its learned merge table, encodes brand-new unseen strings in strict merge-priority order, and asserts `decode(encode(text)) == text`.
deep_assignments.what_you_prove: Why encoding new text MUST apply merges in the exact order they were learned (lowest merge rank first), not greedily by local frequency.
deep_assignments.agent_prompt: I just completed Lesson 2 (Byte-Pair Encoding & Regex Pre-Tokenization) using `lessons/l0-tokens/lab_main.py`.
